title: Clinicopathological characteristics and therapeutic outcomes in patients with non-small cell lung cancer harboring SMARCA4 mutations
author: Yan Liu; Hui Li; Xiang Li; Heran Cui; Rixin Li; Jing Zhu; Hongxia Cui; Ying Liu; Ying Cheng
text:
Abstract
Objective
To investigate the clinical characteristics and impact of SMARCA4 mutations in patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC).
Methods
A total of 2,821 patients with NSCLC who underwent next-generation sequencing were retrospectively included. The frequency and types of SMARCA4 mutations and co-mutations were determined, and the clinical outcomes were assessed.
Results
SMARCA4 mutations were identified in 100 samples (3.54%), and 36% were missense mutations. The most frequent co-mutations were TP53 (67%) and EGFR (31%); 13% of SMARCA4 mutations occurred in samples carried EGFR and TP53 mutations. Notably, 63% SMARCA4 mutations did not present druggable driver mutations. SMARCA4 mutations were most prevalent in males and smokers. Patients with SMARCA4 mutant lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) and EGFR mutations who received EGFR-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKI) as first-line therapy had a lower objective response rate (ORR, 52.94%). In SMARCA4 mutation and EGFR wild-type (wt) NSCLC cohort who received first-line chemotherapy, age (hazard ratio [HR], 3.090; p = 0.026) and performance score (HR, 5.848; p = 0.045) were identified as independent predictors of progression-free survival (PFS). Conversely, brain metastasis was an independent predictor of superior overall survival (HR, 0.188; p = 0.011). The patients with EGFR wt and SMARCA4 mutant Stage IV LUAD who received chemotherapy plus anti-angiogenic therapy significantly improved median PFS compared to chemotherapy alone (p = 0.04).
Conclusions
SMARCA4 mutations were predominantly males and smokers in NSCLC. SMARCA4 mutations conferred a poorer response for EGFR-mutant LUAD subgroups who received EGFR-TKIs. Additionally, chemotherapy plus anti-angiogenesis as first-line therapy may be more effective for Stage IV-SMARCA4 mutant LUAD with EGFR wt.
Keywords: SMARCA4, NSCLC, NGS, clinicopathological characteristics, therapeutic outcomes
KEY MESSAGES
SMARCA4 mutations predominantly occur in males and smokers with NSCLC.
Age, PS, and brain metastasis are independent prognostic factors for patients with SMARCA4 mutant NSCLC who received first-line chemotherapy; Advanced LUAD patients with SMARCA4 mutation had poorer response to first-line EGFR-TKI but had a better response to chemotherapy plus anti-angiogenesis therapy.
Background
Lung cancer is a significant global health concern, it remains the leading cause of cancer-related death globally [1], and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is the most frequent subtype. Despite targeted therapy and immunotherapy having improved therapeutic outcomes for patients with advanced NSCLC, this treatment regime is ineffective in a subset of patients [2]. Several studies have suggested that NSCLC consists of multiple diseases at the molecular biological level [3–6]. Therefore, identification of new biomarkers is urgently required to overcome treatment resistance and prolong survival.
The switch/sucrose non-fermentable (SWI/SNF) complex plays a crucial inhibitory role in cellular proliferation and DNA repair [7]. SWI/SNF-related BRG1/BRM-related factor chromatin remodeling complex subunit ATPase 4 (SMARCA4) is a core regulatory subunit that encodes the transcriptional activator BRG1, which is one of the most common abnormal ATP-dependent catalytic subunits of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex [8,9]. SMARCA4 is involved in transcription processes and it widely acts as a tumor suppressor in lung cancer [10]. Although it has been reported that SMARCA4 is involved in the progression of NSCLC by regulating the non-coding genome through enhancer remodeling [11], the oncogenic or suppressive roles of SMARCA4 are controversial in a variety of cancer types [12,13].
SMARCA4 mutations can impair transcription and DNA damage repair by influencing ATPase activity or chromatin recognition and binding functions, and they are associated with the development of tumors [14]. SMARCA4 mutations are present in 5%–10% of patients with NSCLCs [15–18]. In EGFR-mutant NSCLC, SMARCA4 mutations are involved in epidermal growth factor receptor-tyrosine kinase inhibitor (EGFR-TKI) resistance [19,20]. In addition, in SMARCA4 mutant NSCLC, patients who were KRAS mutation-positive and who were treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) had significantly shorter progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) than patients with KRAS wild-type (wt), identified in a large retrospective study [21]. Recent studies reported that patients with SMARCA4 variants had a poorer response to chemotherapy and a worse prognosis [14,22]. The clinical evidence implied that SMARCA4 mutations represent a new subtype of patients with NSCLC with a worse prognosis[18–22]; thus, optimal therapeutic strategies against SMARCA4 mutant NSCLC requires further investigation. For the detection of SMARCA4-deficient lung cancer, immunohistochemistry (IHC) has been considered to be the standard method but it is unable to identify genetic variations including SMARCA4 missense mutations or rearrangement, which are likely to have changed protein function, Next generation sequencing (NGS) can identify SMARCA4 mutations and co-mutations that regulate SMARCA4 protein expression in NSCLC [23,24]. In this study, the aims were to retrospectively identify the molecular and clinicopathological characteristics of patients with SMARCA4 mutant NSCLC and to determine the correlation between SMARCA4 mutations and clinical outcomes.
Material and methods
Study design and patients
Sequencing data on 2,821 NSCLC cases between June 2018 and December 2023 were retrospectively retrieved from the Jilin Cancer Hospital, including 1,936 paraffin-embedded tumor tissues and 885 circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) from plasma. A total of 100 samples (65 paraffin-embedded tumor tissues and 35 plasma ctDNA samples) from 80 patients with SMARCA4 mutations were screened. The same NGS panel was used to detect 20 matched tumor tissue and ctDNA. The therapy regimes that patients received are shown in Supplementary Table 1. Patients were excluded if they were diagnosed with a malignancy other than NSCLC, including lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC), and NSCLC-not otherwise specified; absence of clinicopathologic data, including sex and sample type; or age <18 years. The Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance score (ranked 0–5 levels) was used to assess health status and treatment tolerance and a higher score indicates poorer status. Response rate (RR) was calculated as complete response + partial response)/number of patients × 100 (%). Survival data included PFS and OS, with commencement of follow-up defined as the time of treatment initiation, and the endpoint defined as treatment progression, death, or the final follow-up. A flowchart of the study design is shown in Figure 1. This study adhered to the ethical principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of Jilin Cancer Hospital (NO: 202501-005-01). Due to the retrospective nature, the requirement for informed consent was waived.
Targeted tumor NGS
Tissue DNA and ctDNA were extracted using the AmoyDx FFPE DNA Kit (AmoyDx, China) and the Circulating DNA Nucleic Acid Extraction Kit (AmoyDx, China), respectively, according to the manufacturer’s protocol. The DNA concentrations were calculated by a Qubit 3.0 Fluorometer (Invitrogen, USA). NGS was performed using somatic mutations of the 520/168 gene panel ((Burning Rock Biotech, China) on the Illumina MiSeq platform (Illumina, USA) and the 1021/59 gene panel (GenePlus, china) on the Gene + Seq2000 platform (BGI, China). The targeted capture sequencing required a mean effective depth of 500X/1000X in tissue DNA and ctDNA, and the coverage uniformity was >90%. The raw data were compared with the human reference genome, hg19, using the sequence alignment software, Burrows-Wheeler Aligner (BWA, version 0.7.10). The Genome Analysis Toolkit (GATK, version 3.2) and VarScan (version 2.4.3) were used for optimization of local alignment, duplicate labeling, and mutating calls. The total mutational burden was calculated as the ratio of the detected non-synonymous mutation count, including single nucleotide variants (SNVs) and small insertions or deletions (Indels) to the total coding region size of the gene panel (1.003 Mb). All SMARCA4 mutations were detected, including missense variant, non-sense variant, frameshift variant, splice_acceptor/donor/region variant, copy number amplification/copy number deletion (cn_amp/del), fusion, inframe_insertion/deletion and stop_gained/lost. Copy number variations (CNV) were estimated using the CNVkit method [25]; the thresholds were set at 3.5, and SNV/indel/SV thresholds were set at 1%, respectively [26]. The different panels were used for biopsies and plasma (Supplementary Table 3).
Statistical analysis
Categorical data were analyzed using the chi-squared test or Fisher’s exact test. Cox proportional hazards model was used to estimate the prognostic factors in the univariable and multivariable models. Survival analysis was performed to determine the association between SMARCA4 mutations and survival using Kaplan–Meier curves and the log-rank test. Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05. The statistical analyses were performed using SPSS (version 22; IBM, USA).
Results
The frequency of SMARCA4 mutations and clinical characteristics
A total of 100 samples from 80 patients had SMARCA4 mutations (3.54%, 100/2,821) with 3.36% (65/1,936) and 3.95% (35/885) detected in tissue and ctDNA samples, respectively. A total of eight types of SMARCA4 mutations were detected, consisting mostly of missense mutations, 40% and 26% in tissue and ctDNA, respectively. The remainder included non-sense (22% in tissue, and 29% in ctDNA), frameshift variant, splice_acceptor/donor/region variant, cn_amp/del, fusion, inframe_insertion/deletion, and stop_gained/lost (Figure 2A, B). There was no significant difference in the types of SMARCA4 mutations between tissues and ctDNA (p > 0.05) (Figure 2C). The matched samples from one individual exhibited the same mutations including SMARCA4, EGFR and TP53 gene.
The SMARCA4 mutation cohort comprised 55 males (68.75%) and 25 females (31.25%), and the median age was 64 years. Of these, 54 patients (73%) were classified as Stage IV and 20 (27%) as Stage I–III. A total of 67 (83.75%) patients had LUAD, five (6.25%) had LUSC, and eight (10%) had other subtypes. Males and smokers accounted for the highest percentage of patients with SMARCA4 mutant NSCLC (Table 1). We analyzed the differences between SMARCA4 mutations and SMARCA4 wt, Males and smokers with NSCLC were more prevalent in SMARCA4 mutations cohorts(p < 0.0001, p = 0.0004, respectively), and associated with a lower Stage IV ratio (p = 0.0044) than patients with NSCLC and SMARCA4 wt (Supplementary Table 2). Furthermore, the proportion of male smoking patients was 78.18% in SMARCA4 mutations cohorts and 52.10% in SMARCA4 wt cohorts, SMARCA4 mutations were prevalent in male smoking patients (p = 0.0003).

Molecular landscape associated with SMARCA4 mutations
The most frequent co-occurring mutations in patients with NSCLC and SMARCA4 mutations were: TP53 (67%, 67/100), EGFR (31%, 31/100), KEAP1 (26%, 26/100), STK11 (24%, 24/100), RB1 (18%, 18/100), and KRAS (13%, 13/100), MET (11%, 11/100). In addition, multiple gene mutations associated with SMARCA4 mutations were identified, with 13% of patients with SMARCA4 mutations also having EGFR and TP53 mutations (Figure 3). Notably, 63% of SMARCA4 mutations occurred in the absence of druggable driver gene mutations.
Efficacy analysis of EGFR-TKI as first-line therapy for patients with EGFR mutant LUAD and with SMARCA4 mutations
The impact of SMARCA4 mutations on the clinical outcomes of EGFR-TKI therapy as first-line therapy in patients with EGFR-mutant LUAD (N = 17) was analyzed. Among the cohort, median PFS (mPFS), mOS, and objective response rate (ORR) were 450 days, 1,184 days, and 52.94%, respectively. Furthermore, the ORR was lower than that previously reported in patients with EGFR mutant NSCLC [27], suggesting that SMARCA4 mutations reduced the response to EGFR-TKI. Furthermore, there was no difference in RR between the TP53 wt subgroup (N = 9) and the TP53 mutation subgroup (N = 8) (Figure 4A). In the SMARCA4 mutation cohort, the mPFS and mOS were 425 days and 1,555 days for EGFR mutations alone, and 265 days and 808 days for EGFR combined TP53 mutations. There were no statistically significant differences in PFS (p = 0.152, HR = 0.46) and OS between the two groups (p = 0.14, HR = 0.44) (Figure 4B, C).
Prognostic value of patients with SMARCA4 mutant NSCLC who received first-line chemotherapy
Clinical prognostic factors were analyzed in the SMARCA4 mutant NSCLC cohort that received first-line chemotherapy (N = 44). The effects of age, sex, smoking status, histopathological diagnosis, and TNM stage were not significant for PFS in the univariate analysis (p > 0.05). Notably, multivariable models revealed that age (p = 0.026, HR = 3.09) and PS (p = 0.045, HR = 5.848) were independent prognostic factors for PFS (Figure 5A); TNM stage and brain metastasis correlated with OS in the univariable analysis (p = 0.032, HR = 3.112; p = 0.003, HR = 0.229), and multivariable analysis revealed that brain metastasis (p = 0.011, HR = 0.188) was a positive independent prognostic factor for OS (Figure 5B). Furthermore, in the Stage IV LUAD subgroup, the patients with SMARCA4 mutations and EGFR wt who received first-line chemotherapy were assigned to one of three groups based on treatment protocols: chemotherapy (n = 6), chemotherapy plus ICIs (n = 9), and chemotherapy plus anti-angiogenic therapy (n = 8). There were no significant differences in treatment efficacy between the three groups (p = 1.000) (Figure 6A). The median PFSs for the chemotherapy group, chemotherapy plus ICIs group, and chemotherapy plus anti-angiogenic therapy group, were 74, 289, and 221 days, respectively, demonstrating a significant difference in PFS (p = 0.031, HR = 0.2). Furthermore, there was a significantly shorter mPFS in the chemotherapy group than in the chemotherapy plus anti-angiogenic therapy group (p = 0.04); however, there was no significant difference between the chemotherapy plus ICI and the anti-angiogenic therapy groups (p = 0.347) (Figure 6B). In contrast, the presence of SMARCA4 mutations had a minimal impact on OS among the three groups (p = 0.41, HR = 0.448 (0.109–1.841)) (Figure 6C). Similarly, the chemotherapy group also had a poorer PFS compared with the SMARCA4 wt cohort (p = 0.0079, HR = 4.676) (Supplementary Figure 1A), and there was no significant between the two groups for patients who received chemotherapy combined with anti-angiogenesis (p = 0.6798, HR = 0.7694) (Supplementary Figure 1B).
Discussion
Therapy targeting NSCLC driver gene mutations can increase the three year OS [28], although patients with advanced NSCLC have a five-year survival rate of only 8.2% [4]. The development of NSCLC involves multiple factors and genes [29]. The prognosis of lung cancer depends on the histopathological type and the molecular characteristics [30,31]; therefore, exploring the molecular mechanisms and identifying key genes will have substantial clinical utility for the treatment of NSCLC. Studies have reported that SMARCA4 mutations are closely associated with the development of bladder urothelial carcinoma, breast-infiltrating ductal carcinoma, gastric cancer, prostate cancer, colon cancer, and other malignant tumors [32]. In addition, SMARCA4 mutations have become biomarkers of poor prognosis in advanced lung cancer and have potential predictive value in anti-tumor treatments [33].
Previous studies have shown that there were SMARCA4 mutations in approximately 5%–10% of patients with NSCLC [14,15,21,34]. The present observational study, using NGS panels, revealed that 3.5% of patients with NSCLC harbored SMARCA4 mutations, which was slightly lower than the findings in previous reports and may be related to the retrospective study cohort and regional differences. In addition, the predominant mutation subtype was a SNV missense mutation, which is consistent with observations in other types of cancer [4,35]. In the present study, the most common concomitant mutations with SMARCA4 mutations were TP53, EGFR, and KEAP1, which is in accordance with the findings reported by Schoenfeld et al. [15], which showed that 56% of SMARCA4 mutations were associated with TP53 mutations. Other studies have also demonstrated that SMARCA4 mutations are concomitant with KRAS and KEAP1 mutations [36,37]. The results of previous studies suggest that SMARCA4 mutations are mutually exclusive to the most commonly targeted oncogenes in NSCLC, where EGFR mutations have the strongest mutual exclusion [24], on the contrary, the findings in the present study indicate that EGFR was the co-mutation driver gene with the highest frequency. We also observed that 63% of SMARCA4 mutations that did not present druggable driver mutations, which is consistent with previous literature[24]. We found that SMARCA4 mutation predominantly occurred in male smokers, and our previous study identified that the smokers with NSCLC showed lower EGFR mutation rate [38], which may partially explain why majority of with SMARCA4 mutations patients did not have concomitant actionable driver mutations.
Consistent with previous reports, in the present study, patients with SMARCA4 mutant NSCLC were more frequently males and smokers [39]. Contrary to the finding of Alessi et al. [21], SMARCA4 mutations were associated with a lower Stage IV ratio. Additionally, the present study indicates that age and PS are poor independent prognostic factors for PFS, and brain metastasis is a superior predictor of OS in patients with SMARCA4 mutant NSCLC and EGFR wt, who received first-line chemotherapy.
The results of recent studies indicate that SMARCA4 mutant NSCLC could be considered to be an independent disease with a poor prognosis [21]. Further investigations will explore optimal treatment strategies that potentially have more benefit in this cohort. Studies on targeted therapy for SMARCA4 mutations are limited but hint at a poor prognosis [20,40]. Interestingly, patients in the LUAD subgroup who received first-line EGFR-TKI therapy, patients with EGFR mutations and SMARCA4 mutations, identified by NGS, had a worse response. However, EGFR mutations, with or without TP53 mutations, had no impact on ORR, mPFS, and mOS in patients receiving EGFR-TKIs. A retrospective study found that first-line ICIs combined with chemotherapy was more effective than chemotherapy alone in patients with SMARCA4-deficient NSCLC [41], which differs from the finding in the present study, that patients with Stage IV disease, SMARCA4 mutations, and EGFR wt, had superior PFS after first-line chemotherapy plus anti-angiogenesis to those after chemotherapy alone, and that there was no difference between chemotherapy plus ICIs and chemotherapy alone. Overall, our findings suggest that patients with SMARCA4 mutations exhibit different clinicopathological characteristics and a poor response to chemotherapy compared with patients with SMARCA4 wt, thus, it should be considered as an independent subtype of NSCLC. patients with SMARCA4 mutations require different therapeutic strategies to improve survival outcomes, and combination therapy has potential to improve the prognosis.
There are some limitations of the present study. The data were derived from a retrospective analysis, and the treatment regimens were not consistent due to clinical complexity. In addition, the patient cohorts were sourced from a single cancer center and remain geographic limitations, the data may not fully represent all the region. Furthermore, differences in the NGS detection panel between tissue and ctDNA may limit the comparability of the cohorts. The panel-based NGS could not differentiate between activated or suppressed molecular patterns, in this series. The data revealed significant associations between SMARCA4 mutations and survival outcomes, however, further investigations into the molecular mechanisms that might explain this observation were not performed. Multi-center, prospective studies are required, including functional studies.
Conclusions
The present study, revealed that patients with NSCLC and SMARCA4 mutations are predominantly males and smokers. SMARCA4 mutations predicted a poor response to EGFR-TKI in patients with EGFR mutant LUAD. Furthermore, age, PS, and brain metastasis are associated with survival outcomes in patients with SMARCA4 mutant NSCLC who received first-line chemotherapy. Finally, first-line chemotherapy plus anti-angiogenesis showed promising efficacy in patients with Stage IV LUAD, SMARCA4 mutations, and EGFR wt.
